content.title: Meet the four astronauts on NASA’s Artemis II moon mission
content.text: Three military pilots and a scientist who spent a year in Antarctica – including the winter – are preparing to launch on a 10-day journey around the moon.The four astronauts on NASA’s Artemis II mission won’t land on the lunar surface, but they’ll come closer than any other humans in more than 50 years.Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.ONLY 25¢Their mission will test the spacecraft’s life support systems, provide a unique opportunity for science and prepare NASA for future moon landings.Article continues below this ad“We are doing this to fulfill a promise to the American people that we will return to the moon,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said during a news conference.The Artemis II mission is commanded by NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman. NASA astronaut Victor Glover is the pilot, and NASA astronaut Christina Hammock Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen are mission specialists.Wiseman, Glover and Hansen are pilots who earned advanced STEM degrees before becoming astronauts. Koch, who also has an advanced STEM degree, developed space science instruments and worked in remote scientific field engineering.These astronauts live and work in the Houston area, and they’ve spent three years training for this historic mission.Article continues below this adGlover will be the first Black man to fly around the moon. Koch will be the first woman, and Hansen will be the first Canadian.If they launch April 1-4, their trajectory should take them farther from Earth than humans have ever traveled, surpassing the Apollo 13 mission that traveled 248,655 miles from home.These firsts help people notice the mission, Koch said, but they’re not top priorities for the crew.“It's not about farthest, first, fastest, longest,” she said during a news conference. “It's about the teamwork and the work that went into that. And the dedication that it took to take on those big challenges.” The Artemis II mission is expected to launch Wednesday from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The two-hour launch window opens at 5:24 p.m. Central time. Meet the four astronauts who will be onboard:NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman poses for a portrait. Wiseman is part of NASA's Artemis II moon mission.NASA/Josh ValcarcelReid Wiseman, CommanderHometown: Baltimore, Md.Age: 50Education: Bachelor’s degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; master’s degree in systems engineering from Johns Hopkins University; certificate of space systems from U.S. Naval Postgraduate SchoolMilitary experience: Naval aviator and test pilotDays in space: 165Artemis II personal items: Blank piece of paper and pencilWiseman was selected for astronaut training in 2009, and he went to the International Space Station on Russia’s Soyuz rocket in 2014. He spent 165 days in space.His path to NASA began in the Navy. Wiseman was commissioned through the ROTC after graduating from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and he became a naval aviator in 1999. He later graduated from the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and worked flight test programs that included the F-35 Lightning II, F-18 weapons separation and the T-45 Goshawk, according to his NASA bio.While on the International Space Station, Wiseman led two spacewalks and spent nearly 13 hours outside of the orbiting platform. One of his fondest memories is laughing with crewmates.“When you laugh in space to the point where you cry tears of joy,” Wiseman said during a news conference, “they just stick right in your eyeballs. And I always thought that was hilarious.”NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman is the Artemis II commander. He's shown in various photos from Artemis II training, NASA events and his time on the International Space Station.Top left: Raquel Natalicchio/Staff photographer; Other three: NASAWiseman was chief of the astronaut office, responsible for managing astronaut resources and assigning crew members to missions, from 2020 through 2022. Of his many jobs, Wiseman says his time as an only parent has been the most challenging and rewarding, according to his NASA bio.His wife Carroll died from cancer in 2020, and Wiseman has been raising their two daughters. One is in college and the other is in high school.He’d struggle to leave them on a six-month mission to the International Space Station, Wiseman said. But a 10-day mission feels more digestible.“I couldn't be more proud of them,” he said in an interview. “I know it's not easy. I know I could give them an easier life, but they are very resilient.”The Artemis II astronauts have been allotted one pound – shared among the four crew members – for personal items. Wiseman said he’s bringing a blank piece of paper and a pencil to write his thoughts.He hopes the ride home will be as energizing as his return in the Soyuz capsule.“It's an impressive ride,” he said during a news conference. “When you land, the first thing I thought when I landed was, ‘I would go do that immediately … I want that ride again.’ And so I hope that's what we feel when we splash down on Artemis II. That will be a great moment.”NASA astronaut Victor Glover poses for a portrait. Glover is part of NASA's Artemis II moon mission.NASA/Josh ValcarcelVictor Glover, pilotHometown: Pomona, Calif.Age: 49Education: Bachelor’s degree in general engineering from California Polytechnic State University; master’s degree in flight test engineering from Air University; master’s degree in systems engineering from Naval Postgraduate School and master’s degree in military operational art and science from Air University; certificate in legislative studies at Georgetown UniversityMilitary experience: Naval aviator and test pilotDays in space: 168Artemis II personal items: Bible and heirlooms for his wife and daughtersGlover was selected for astronaut training in 2013 and went to the International Space Station on NASA’s SpaceX Crew-1 mission in November 2020. He spent 168 days in space.Born in Pomona, Calif., Glover attended Cal Poly on a wrestling scholarship. He also played football while earning his bachelor’s degree in general engineering.He joined the Navy and later became a test pilot, working on various weapons systems for the F/A-18 Hornet, Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler.Glover has accumulated 3,500 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft. He’s also completed more than 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions, according to his NASA bio. He was a legislative fellow in the U.S. Senate when selected as an astronaut candidate.NASA astronaut Victor Glover is the Artemis II pilot. He's shown in various photos from Artemis II training, NASA events and his time on the International Space Station.Top left: Raquel Natalicchio/Staff Photographer; Other three: NASAHis spaceflight, the Crew-1 mission, was the second crewed flight of a SpaceX Dragon. Glover completed four spacewalks during his nearly six-month stay on the International Space Station.And while his full name is Victor J. Glover, Jr., astronauts often call him “IKE.” This nickname was given to Glover by a commanding officer in the Navy, and it stands for “I Know Everything.”“I truly have never met a human being with a memory like his,” Wiseman said of Glover. “He truly remembers, literal word for word, details in conversations from years ago. I've learned through working with him that precision of language is very important. He's made me such a better astronaut because of that.”Glover doesn’t like to say that he’s excited for Artemis II. For him, excitement can become a distraction. He prefers to be focused. However, he is hoping for a moment of awe similar to what he felt before the Crew-1 launch.“I'm focused, but I look forward to a moment like that,” he said.For Artemis II, he’s bringing a Bible and heirlooms for his wife Dionna and their four daughters.NASA astronaut Christina Hammock Koch poses for a portrait. Koch is part of NASA's Artemis II moon mission.NASA/Josh ValcarcelChristina Hammock Koch, mission specialist Hometown: Native of Grand Rapids, Mich.; grew up in Jacksonville, N.C.Age: 47Education: Bachelor’s degrees in electrical engineering and physics and a master’s degree in electrical engineering from North Carolina State UniversityPre-NASA experience: Space science instrument development and remote scientific field engineeringDays in space: 328Artemis II personal items: Handwritten notes from loved onesKoch was selected for astronaut training in 2013 and went to the International Space Station in Russia’s Soyuz spacecraft in March 2019. She spent 328 days in space, the longest single spaceflight for a woman, and participated in the first all-female spacewalks.Koch is a native of Grand Rapids, Mich., but grew up in Jacksonville, N.C. She earned electrical engineering and physics degrees from North Carolina State University and studied abroad at the University of Ghana.Before becoming an astronaut, she helped develop space instruments and did remote scientific field work in Antarctica, Greenland, Alaska and American Samoa.Koch was working at NOAA’s American Samoa Observatory when she was chosen for astronaut training. She trained in the same class as Glover.Growing up, Koch said she had many female role models from NASA: Sally Ride, the first American woman in space; Mae Jemison, the first woman of color in space; Kathryn Sullivan, the first American woman to complete a spacewalk; Eileen Collins and Pam Melroy, space shuttle commanders. She was also inspired by civil rights leader Ella Baker, according to a Houston Chronicle interview from 2023.NASA astronaut Christina Hammock Koch is a mission specialist on NASA's Artemis II mission. She is shown in various photos from Artemis II training, NASA events and her time on the International Space Station.Bottom right: Kirk Sides/Staff Photographer; Other three: NASA“I had a lot of role models of all different kinds, and it's important to me to pay homage to those people,” she said in an interview last year. “It's also important to me to remember that might be my role now in inspiring the next generation of explorers.” But Koch said superlatives don’t always tell the full story. For instance, many people don’t know – or recall – that the first all-female spacewalk was a contingency spacewalk. It was needed to swap out a failed component.“We executed it a week after it was conceived. That is completely unheard of in the space industry,” Koch said in 2023. “Making a spacewalk is normally a several-year process where it gets practiced in the Neutral Buoyancy Lab many, many times. Every little thing is choreographed.”Koch completed six spacewalks during her mission. Her scientific highlights included growing protein crystals for pharmaceutical research and testing 3D biological printers in microgravity, according to her NASA bio.Wiseman described Koch as an understander. “She wants to know everything that is going to happen,” Wiseman said. “She's always prepared for everything that is coming, and that helps our crew out immensely. She catches things that no one else on the crew would ever catch because she is an understander.” Koch is married to Robert Koch. She’s using her personal allotment on Artemis II to bring hand-written notes from friends and family. She’s excited to see how this mission could benefit science, technology development and STEM inspiration.“The thing I love about the moon is that it's not just a beacon for exploration,” Koch said. “It has benefits. That's actually why we're racing toward it.”Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen poses for a portrait. Hansen is part of NASA's Artemis II moon mission.NASA/Josh ValcarcelJeremy Hansen, mission specialistHometown: London, OntarioAge: 50Education: Bachelor's degree in space science and a master’s degree in physics from Royal Military College of Canada.Military experience: Fighter pilotDays in space: 0Artemis II personal items: Moon pendants for his familyHansen was selected for astronaut training in 2009 through Canada’s third astronaut recruitment campaign. This will be his first trip into space.Hansen was born in London, Ontario, and grew up on a farm near Ailsa Craig, Ontario. He joined an aviation youth program, the Royal Canadian Air Cadets, at 12 years old. He then received his Air Cadet glider pilot wings and his private pilot license at 16 and 17, respectively. He later joined the Canadian Armed Forces. Hansen graduated from the Royal Military College of Canada with his bachelor’s and master’s degrees and became a CF-18 fighter pilot.Canada has recruited 14 astronauts through four campaigns since 1983. Hansen’s training was conducted alongside U.S. and Japanese astronauts. He was in the same class as Wiseman.After his training, Hansen worked in Houston’s mission control as the capcom who relays messages between ground teams and astronauts on the International Space Station.He also participated in two extreme space simulations. Hansen spent six days underground in the European Space Agency’s CAVES program and seven days underwater at the Aquarius research station as a member of NEEMO 19, according to his Canadian Space Agency bio.Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen is a mission specialist on NASA's Artemis II mission. He is shown in various photos from Artemis II events and training.Top right: Raquel Natalicchio/Staff photographer; Other three: NASANASA, he said, has been an amazing leader in space, and he praised the agency for making room for others.He also praised Canada for earning its spot on the Artemis II mission.“It wasn't a gift. You earned it,” Hansen said during a news conference. “You have used strategic investments, and you have innovated and created things like Canadarm … that have put us in this position where we can earn our place on the global stage. And that's extraordinary. That is our can-do attitude.” Wiseman praised Hansen’s youthful ambition. He described him as creative and inquisitive.If Hansen took apart a pen, learned all about it and then put it back together, Wiseman said he could probably use that information to help create a tool that would save the mission in an emergency.“He has shown that time and time again in (simulations),” Wiseman said. “Sometimes you're like, ‘Jeremy, just please stop playing around. Let's just focus.’ But then all of a sudden, a week later, you're like, ‘Thank you for doing that. We learned so much out of that.’”Hansen is using his personal space for moon pendants he gave his wife, Catherine, and their three children. And while he knows this mission won’t solve the world’s problems, he hopes that, just for a moment, the planet’s 8 billion people will pause to appreciate the achievement.“Just having humanity stop for a moment and say, ‘Wow, look at what we can do when we work together,’” Hansen said. “Let’s just set goals to do a better job of that on this planet today.”Start your day and stay informed with essential Houston news.
